en: Biography of the Great Virtuous One, the Imperial Preceptor of the Three Reigns at Qinglong Monastery of the Great Tang:
Our late Master, the Venerable Huiguo, was surnamed Ma. He was a native of Guiming Township, Wannian County, Jingzhao Prefecture.
At the age of nine, he entered the Shengfo Monastery; thus, for three reigns...
The State Preceptor and Inner Chamber Reciter, the purple-robed śramaṇa whose name was Venerable Tánzhēn,
resolved to study the scriptures and reached the age of seventeen.
He served as the preceptor for the Empress Dowager;
he constantly remained within the inner palace chapel,
reciting mantras without ever leaving.
Thereupon, at the age of nineteen, he sought to receive the transmission of the *Mahāpratisarā* and other mantras from the Tripiṭaka Master at Xingshan Monastery.
After receiving the instruction and the consecration of scattering flowers from the Tripitaka Master,
he attained the state of a Bodhisattva who turns the wheel of Dharma.
His Upādhyāya said:
"In the kingdom of South India,
I obtained this Honored One by scattering flowers;
it is no different from how it is now."
After my passing,
you shall propagate the Great Teaching of the Dhāraṇī,
no different from me.
Furthermore, in the third lunar month of the eighth year of the Dali era,
an imperial edict was issued at Cien Monastery.
Established at the Fangdeng (Vaipulya) Bodhimanda.
The Preceptor of the Holy Buddha Courtyard respectfully received the imperial decree from Cien Monastery.
At the site of the Vaipulya Bodhimanda, there were two young monks,
both twenty years of age and capable of receiving full ordination.
I have not yet dared to take it upon myself to shave the head of this renunciant.
I humbly beg for Your Majesty’s compassionate favor to permit me to return to the monastery.
He gave him two young attendants,
as well as the precept robes and alms bowl;
he also bestowed upon him a single sword by imperial decree.
In front of the Great Buddha Hall of Qinglong Monastery,
the imperial decree was bestowed upon the two novices of the Upādhyāya for their tonsure;
they were each granted two sets of monastic robes, alms bowls, and other requisites.
Having been granted an official edict permitting him to reside at the temple,
the Heavenly Envoy escorted the Upādhyāya to Ci’en Temple. Upon completion of this,
he returned to the palace to offer thanks for the imperial decree.
I, a humble monk of this realm,
thank Your Majesty for your sacred compassion in granting two youths ordination and bestowing upon them robes,
alms bowls, and razors.
The official notification and the messenger sent it to the ritual precinct of Ci'en Monastery.
Once the conferral of the precepts was completed,
this humble monk could not help but offer his deepest congratulations.
Having completed the conferral of the precepts at the age of twenty-two,
he further [received them] from the master Xuanchao, a disciple of the Tripitaka Master Vajrabodhi (Wuweizang).
He requested the transmission of the Mahāyoga Great Teachings of the Mahāvairocana Tathāgata’s Matrix of Great Compassion (Mahākaruṇāgarbha),
as well as the Mahāyoga methods of Susiddhi and the various yoga rites for the Honored Ones.
He received personal oral instructions from each of them in turn.
Furthermore, at the residence of the Tripiṭaka Master at Daxingshan Temple,
he requested and received the transmission of the *Vajraśekhara-mahāyoga-mahātantrarāja-sūtra*.
The secret mudrās of the yoga of the various deities were personally received through direct instruction;
they are those obtained by my former master while within [the sacred precinct].
We have respectfully offered all these gifts to the Tripiṭaka Upādhyāya as an expression of gratitude for the favor of bestowing the Dharma;
we remain constantly at your feet.
Restricting his diet and setting a deadline,
he recited it several times daily;
this continued until he was twenty-five years old.
By special imperial decree, he was summoned to enter the palace;
at that time, an edict was issued for him to come to the Changsheng Hall.
In response to the question,
"What efficacy does the Master possess?
Jiatian said:
The humble monk has not yet produced any efficacious results.
Having received the imperial decree, he immediately acted with sincerity at that time and summoned eight youths.
Through the empowerment of *kōshō* (invocation and summoning),
whatever was requested by imperial decree was entirely accomplished; the turning of the vase and the joining of the bamboo were likewise successfully achieved.
The Emperor was greatly pleased.
In the tenth year of the Dali era,
at that very temple, he...
A separate imperial edict granted one East Pagoda Temple,
wherein a Vairocana Consecration Mandala was established,
and seven monks were stationed to perform recitations.
In the eleventh year of the Dali era,
he performed the empowerment for Emperor Daizong,
and [the illness] was immediately cured.
An imperial decree granted him a pair of purple robes;
he respectfully declined to accept them and returned them immediately.
The imperial edict stated:
"I have already bestowed purple robes upon you, Master;
how can you refuse to accept them?"
He replied,
"I am but a humble monk of this realm;
to be granted the purple robe is a burden I can hardly bear."
He immediately joined his palms and accepted it,
saying: "Since my Preceptor was previously granted the purple robe by the Emperor,
it is not fitting for a disciple to be on equal footing with his Master."
The Emperor said,
"Master, you are truly great in filial piety;
this was my fault."
The Imperial Edict stated:
"Regarding those of other lineages and different surnames who stand above [the imperial kin],
they maintain a heart of reverence, obedience, and filial piety."
Thereafter, as he was deemed worthy to serve as State Preceptor,
the Emperor bestowed upon him a pair of coarse cloth robes.
By imperial decree,
the princess Hwayang was blessed with healing after three days.
Later, during the hours of Shen and Wei,
the Princess suddenly fell silent;
the Emperor and his palace attendants [were struck with wonder].
Facing forward,
the Upādhyāya reported,
"It is hot at this time."
He looked toward the foot of the steps where the palace attendants were gathered and said,
"If you would briefly grant this humble monk your empowerment, she shall immediately recover.
Thereupon, the princess was cured.
His words were clear and distinct;
the Emperor was greatly pleased and bestowed upon him one hundred bolts of silk.
A pair of robes.
Thank you for the imperial decree.
I, a humble monk within this single realm, [humbly submit].
I thank Your Sacred Benevolence for the gift of silk and garments.
I am overcome with gratitude and offer my highest congratulations. On the third day, I orally petitioned to transfer the Princess.
Regarding all the money and goods bestowed during the Dali era:
Over one thousand strings of cash were entirely used for meritorious works at the base of the stupa.
In the thirteenth year of the Dali era.
He petitioned for permission to tour the Southern Terrace twice, once before and once after;
in accordance with the Master’s request,
the Upādhyāya [performed rites] at Guanyin Terrace.
While he was thus reciting and maintaining mindfulness for a long time into the night,
the Great Sage Avalokiteśvara appeared.
Within a great lunar disc,
he manifests a vast physical form,
with radiance like that of the midday sun.
The auspicious clouds were pure and bright;
at that time, several hundred thousand people from afar gazed upon them together in worship.
In the thirteenth year of the Dali era,

an imperial edict was issued concerning the late Tripiṭaka Master of the Inner Altar of Changsheng Hall, who had transmitted the Dharma and conferred the empowerment during the three daily assemblies.
The edict addressed Huiguo as follows:
After the demise of the Upādhyāya of the Tripiṭaka,
[the Master] thought that the Buddha-dharma would have no further transmission; however,
he heard that his teacher had mastered the Great Dharma.
In general, while attending to state affairs at the side of the Venerable Huishang,
I received the Dharma-gate of Recitation,
but I have largely forgotten it.
On another day, when he descended from his seat to inquire after him,
this was precisely the occasion for the Master’s formal installation.
On the fifteenth day of the tenth month in the thirteenth year of the Dali era.
Proclaimed by Li Xiancheng of Gao.
At the beginning of the Jianzhong era,
there was a monk from the kingdom of Ho-ling named Bianhong.
From his own country,
he brought a set of bronze gongs and offered them to the temple of the Holy Buddha.
Two pairs of conch shells and four bronze *kundika* flasks were respectfully offered to the Upādhyāya.
He made full offerings and sought the transmission of the Great Dharma of the Womb Realm Vairocana.
This was in the second year of the Jianguan era.
The monk Hye-il of Silla presented tribute from his own country to the Upādhyāya.
I requested and received the *Tattvasaṃgraha*, the *Vajradhātu*, the *Susiddhi*, and so forth,
as well as thirty fundamental texts on the yoga of various deities;
these have all been bestowed.
Having mastered [the teachings] in later years,
he returned to his native country and widely propagated the Great Teaching.
Through his sincere devotion, he abstained from grain and maintained his recitations until *siddhi* manifested before him;
he subsequently ascended to the heavens during the day and paid homage within the royal palace of Central India.
He sought that Dharma.
A voice from the sky said: "In the Great Tang country to the west, there is a secret Dharma;
that Dharma is at Qinglong Monastery."
In the same year, a monk from the kingdom of Silla named Wozhen was granted the teachings on the Garbhadhātu-maṇḍala Vairocana and the mantra-recitation rites for the various deities;
this continued until the fifth year of the Zhenyuan era.
He traveled to the kingdom of Central India,
where he obtained the Sanskrit manuscript of the Mahāvairocana Sūtra and other scriptures; however,
he passed away in the kingdom of Tufan (Tibet).
The disciples of this temple are the monks Gīmmyō,
Gīmitsu, and Gītei.
At the same time, he requested from his preceptor thirty scriptures, including the *Vairocana-garbha-tantra* and the *Susiddhi-sāgara-sūtra*.
This was in the fifth year of the Zhenyuan era.
By Imperial Decree, seven monks were ordered to pray for rain at the Great Buddha Hall of this temple.
On the seventh night, when the rain was sufficient, each monk was granted one bundle of silk.
Ten strings of tea were presented as a token of gratitude.
By imperial decree, the Right Guard escorted the true body [of the Buddha] into the palace.
On the □ day of the fourth month in the sixth year of the Zhenyuan era,
an imperial edict was issued ordering the monk Huiguo to enter the palace at the Changsheng Hall.
He remained for more than seventy days to recite mantras for the sake of the state,
after which he was released and returned home.
Each person was granted thirty bolts of silk and twenty strings of tea. Thereafter,
they were divided into shifts for the upper and lower sections.
He was granted seasonal garments and provisions for the three festivals. That year,
Prime Minister Du Huang-chang and Prime Minister Wei personally came to receive the *abhiṣeka*.
He studied and maintained the recitation.
He petitioned for a second tour of inspection,
and by imperial decree, it was granted accordingly.
He served as the Great Virtuous One (Dade) at Chongguansi from the ninth year of the Zhenyuan era until the thirteenth year.
Yiheng, Yiyi, and Yizheng.
Yi Xuan, Yi Cao, and Yi Yun.
Wisdom flourishes;
righteousness evokes compassion;
conduct is firm.
Yuantong, Yilun, and Yibo.
Yirun. His lay disciples included Wu Yin,
Kaipei, and others.
Approximately fifty people were studying the Dharma.
In the fifth month of the fourteenth year of the Zhenyuan era,
there was a great drought.
In the upper half of the fifth lunar month,
he was commissioned by imperial decree to pray for rain;
on the seventh day, [it fell].
Within the inner sanctuary,
he single-mindedly and diligently maintained his recitation;
when the days for praying for rain were completed, [the rain fell].
I thank you for the gift of one bundle of silk and ten strings of tea.
We, the monastic subjects,
have long lacked meritorious conduct;
yet Heaven has sent down sweet rain.
The Emperor was moved by this transformation.
The monks and others thanked him for the silk and tea,
expressing their boundless gratitude and congratulations from the depths of their hearts.
In the eighteenth year of the Zhenyuan era,
during the latter half of the eighth month,
he performed the empowerment ritual for the Crown Prince.
He recovered after three days.
To each was granted twenty bolts of silk, fifty rolls of Wu-ling gauze,
and twenty strings of tea.
We, the humble monks of this realm,
thank Your Majesty for the gracious gift of silk, brocade, and tea;
we are overwhelmed with the deepest joy and gratitude.
On the sixteenth day of the eleventh month in the winter of the sixteenth year,
the general Jiao Hu of the Shenwei Army invited the Upādhyāya to his military residence for offerings.
Together with a portrait of the Upādhyāya,
these were decorated and sent to the monastery in the eighteenth year.
The Upādhyāya fell ill and his condition gradually grew grave;
he submitted a formal petition requesting to retire,
and by imperial decree was granted leave to return home.
Furthermore, let the temple rest for a time;
it is my intention to preserve this from beginning to end,
so Zhan may not yet depart.
In the middle of the eighth month of that year,
he relinquished his robes and alms bowl,
entrusting them for use to seven people, including Yiming.
In the nineteenth year of the Zhenyuan era,
the Japanese monk Kūkai,
by imperial decree, brought a monastic robe (*manna*) and over five hundred strings of currency as national tribute.
Having honored the Upādhyāya,
they dedicated everything toward the adornment of the maṇḍala for offerings,
seeking to receive the initiation into the Mahākaruṇā-garbha-vajradhātu.
Together with the yoga teachings of the various deities,
he received fifty volumes of scriptures;
at that moment, he beheld the realm of the Brahma-syllable *Aṃ*, the sun and moon disks.
It appeared in his mouth.
On the fifth day of the eighth month of the twenty-first year of the Zhenyuan era.
The era was changed to Yongzhen Year 1.
On the fifteenth day of the twelfth month,
[the coffin] was placed with the head to the north, and the funeral rites were concluded.
On the seventeenth day of the first month in the first year of the Yuanhe era,
approximately one thousand disciples, both monastic and lay,
escorted [the remains] to the funeral.
He arrived at the side of the stupa of National Master Longyuan in Mengcun.
Subsequently, on the twenty-first day of the eighth month of the second year of the Baoli era,
Yi-i [recorded this].
He deeply penetrated the meaning [of the teachings] by the banks of the Dan and San rivers.
The stele is located in Lincun.
A stupa was constructed and he was reinterred in the fourth year of the Kaicheng era.
On the thirteenth day of the first month,
the Japanese monk Enkō brought religious robes and tokens of faith.

The manuscript colophon states: "Completed on the twenty-fifth day of the eighth month in the year of the Great Age Xinmao (1171), at the hour of Xu; this is the Zhongchuan edition. On the final day of the ninth month in the year of Guan Ying (1320)."
Having completed the transcription at the monastic quarters of the West Cloister in Tōshōji,
I have compiled them into a single set for my own reference.
*Ken* (Viewing) [Signature/Colophon]: Revised by Kaō Kaien, Junior Bishop (Shōsōjū). Ryōshin.
